title: Predicting the end
hook: people have set dates, like the Millerites; Jesus said no one knows the hour

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's letter to grieving friends: caught up together, and so ever with the Lord. Your line was ever with the lord. Who did you send comfort to? Day one thousand three hundred seventeen.

A preacher named William Miller sat down with the book of Daniel and a lot of arithmetic, and worked out when Christ would return. People believed him, and among his followers a day was fixed. They told their neighbors, and waited. The day came. The sun went down on it like any other. His followers gave what came next a name: the Great Disappointment. Others have set dates too, and each one has come and gone. And yet the Gospels record Jesus saying something very plain about that day, plain enough to fit on a sticky note.

First, the plain words. In Matthew, on the Mount of Olives, Jesus says: "But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only." In Mark, the King James text adds, "neither the Son." Christians have explained that line in different ways, but the sentence itself is hard to miss: not you, not the angels. Second, the thief. Paul tells the Thessalonians "the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night." A thief doesn't send a schedule. And in Acts, when the disciples ask the risen Jesus whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel, he answers: "It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power." Then he's taken up, and two men in white ask them, "why stand ye gazing up into heaven?" Third, what to do instead. "Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come." And right after, Jesus tells of a servant left in charge of a household: "Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing." Doing what? His job. Feeding the household on time. In these chapters, watching doesn't mean staring at the sky with a calculator. It means being found at your work, faithful, whenever the knock comes. Fourth, fear. Date-setting can run on dread and on excitement, and both can pull people out of their ordinary lives. Not knowing the hour sends attention back to this one: the people in the house, the work in front of you.
screen: `NOT THE ANGELS, BUT THE FATHER ONLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one fear about the end. It might be about the world, or about your own life: a diagnosis, a deadline, a headline. Settle, and breathe. Name the fear once, quietly. Then picture setting it down on a table beside you, like a bag you've carried too long. Don't argue with it. Just let it sit there while you breathe. Then bring your attention to this hour: the room, the sounds, the next ordinary thing you'll do. If you pray, you can hand the fear over to God. If you don't, just leave it on the table. The bell holds the time.
Predicting the end. People have set dates, and the dates have passed. In the Gospels Jesus says of that day and hour, no one knows.

Your line: no one knows the hour. Today, when worry about the future pulls at you, do the next small task in front of you well, as if being found doing it is enough. Day one thousand three hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Churches that say the Nicene Creed confess that Christ will come again, and some Christians read Matthew 24 in Advent as a call to watchfulness rather than a timetable.

original.note: Greek: hour, the set time. "of that day and hour knoweth no man", Matthew 24:36.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Bible hides a date for the end, if you can crack the code.
what it means: Jesus says no one knows the day or hour, and that watching means being found faithful at your work.
what a scholar hears: hora, the hour; and Mark 13:32's "neither the Son", a line Christians have explained in different ways.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's year for the Millerites (1844) and any follower numbers were left out of the voice; the hook field drops 'many'. William Miller, his calculation from Daniel, and the 'Great Disappointment' are stated without dates. Confirm the description.
'Others have set dates, before Miller and since' is a general historical claim with no source cited; confirm or cut.
Mark 13:32 'neither the Son' is noted as explained by Christians in different ways, without detail. Confirm.
Acts 1:11: the speakers are 'two men ... in white apparel' (Acts 1:10). Confirm the paraphrase.
howItsDone: churches that say the Nicene Creed confess Christ will come again; some read Matthew 24 in Advent. Confirm.

Editor: the hook no longer says Miller himself fixed a single day (he gave a span; the final day was fixed among his followers) and drops 'settled their affairs'; 'before Miller and since' became 'others have set dates too'; Mark's 'neither the Son' is now tied to the King James text rather than 'Mark goes further'; the fork's 'work it out from Daniel' distractor was replaced, since Matthew 24:15 does cite Daniel.

Audit 2026-10-02: Acts 1:6 paraphrase now keeps the disciples' actual question (restore the kingdom to Israel); myth 3 rewritten, since Matthew 24:32-33 does speak of watching for signs (the fig tree), so 'watching never means signs' overstated the text.
